Reading Blueprints: Symbols, Scales, Legends, Floor Plans, Riser Diagrams

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 5 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The foreman unrolls the telecom sheet on the hood of the truck and says, "Count me the drops on the third floor." A drawing is a compressed set of instructions, and the first skill is knowing where to look.

The frame of every sheet

  • Title block: the sheet number, the project, the date, and the revision. Always confirm you hold the latest revision.
  • Legend: decodes every symbol on the sheet.
  • General notes: the rules that apply to the whole sheet, such as cable type or mounting height.

Scales

A drawing is smaller than the building. An architectural scale reads in feet and inches, an engineering scale reads in decimal feet, and a metric scale reads as a ratio. Use the scale printed in the title block and measure along the route, not in a straight line.

The sheet types

Sheet                      What it shows
Floor plan                 outlets, rooms, and pathways on one level
Reflected ceiling plan     what is in the ceiling: lights, devices, access points
Riser diagram              how the floors connect, and the backbone between TRs
Details                    enlarged views: a firestop, a rack, a mounting
Schedules                  tables listing outlets, cable, or equipment

Telecom symbols

Outlets carry symbols for voice, data, or both, and a number or a count beside the symbol tells you how many ports. Pathways are drawn as lines with their own symbols: conduit, cable tray, and ladder rack each have a line style the legend decodes, usually with a size or tag beside it. A telecom room (TR) is drawn as a room outline with a boxed label, and an equipment room or entrance facility is tagged the same way, so you can find the room every run ends in. Each outlet also has an ID such as a room and port, and the ID is what you label.

When the drawing and the field disagree

A wall is in the wrong place or a duct blocks the route. Stop. Do not guess. Ask the foreman, who asks the designer in writing. Document the change on your as-built set so the record matches what was built.

Tip: take a photo of the revision block before you carry a sheet to the job. Old rolls stay on trucks for months.
Exam tip: when the drawing and the field disagree, the FIRST step is to stop and ask the designer, then document the change.
Remember
Read the title block, the revision, and the legend first; count outlets from the symbols; and when the field disagrees, stop, ask, and document.
Deeper explanation

Reading Blueprints: Symbols, Scales, Legends, Floor Plans, Riser Diagrams, explained slowly

A sample legend, decoded

Every sheet has a legend. On the sample telecom sheet below, read the legend first and the drawing second. Each symbol means exactly what the legend says on that sheet, and the legend on the next job may use the same shape for something else.

Symbol               Meaning on this sheet
Triangle, one fill   voice outlet, one port
Square, one fill     data outlet, one port
Triangle and square  voice and data outlet, two ports
Circle with W        wireless access point on the ceiling
Heavy dashed line    cable tray above the ceiling
TR in a box          telecom room

Counting outlets from a floor plan

Take the sample floor: four offices along one side, an open area in the middle, and a conference room.

Room           Symbol                            Outlets (ports)
Office 301     one voice and data                2 ports
Office 302     one voice and data                2 ports
Office 303     one voice and data                2 ports
Office 304     one voice and data                2 ports
Open area      six data squares                  6 ports
Conference     two voice and data                4 ports
Hall ceiling   two access points                 2 ports
Total                                            20 ports

The count is 20 ports. Check the schedule: it should list the same 20 outlet IDs. If the floor plan says 20 and the schedule says 19, the drawing and the schedule disagree. Do not guess which is right.

Scale in practice

Suppose the title block says 1/8 in = 1 ft. A line on the sheet 2 in long represents 16 ft of building. Measure the route along the pathway, then add the vertical drops and the slack. A route that scales to 80 ft on the sheet can be 95 ft after drops and slack.

When the field differs

Stop, ask the designer in writing, and mark the change on your as-built set. The revision, the schedule, and the field must agree when you finish.

Remember: legend first, counts from the symbols, measure the route not the line, and write down every change.
